articles.title: This Is the Best Christmas Movie for You, According to Your Zodiac Sign
articles.content:
There’s an eternal debate swirling around whether Die Hard is actually a Christmas movie, but you know the answer, Aries. You love a good fight, and you will happily present your detailed, 10-point argument to anyone who will listen. Heck, you’d watch this flick just because of the debate behind it. Though, let’s be honest, as a sign ruled by war-driven Mars, you really love the idea of mixing a beloved, sedate holiday with an impromptu hostage takeover.
Another reason you’ll gravitate toward this one? You tend to operate under main-character energy, so you’ll relate to the fact that John McClane stumbles into the middle of a terrorist plot and is somehow the only one who can help. That would totally be you, Aries, and now you’re locked in. Bonus: Because it’s packed with nonstop action, you won’t have time to get bored. Yes, we know you only make it through half of most Christmas movies before jumping to the next thing. Yippee-ki-yay—yeah, we’re not going to finish that phrase. It’s Christmas!
You’re all about maintaining tradition, Taurus; it’s one of the things that makes you the most stubborn sign out there. It’s also why Clark’s unwavering commitment to the perfect Christmas in Christmas Vacation is so classically you. The lights will work, the family will gather and this will be a Christmas to remember! And that moment when Clark devolves into destitute mania after opening that envelope from his boss will totally resonate with you. Overall, his commitment to the holiday through thick and thin is what will draw you to this flick, since you totally get the idea of toughing something out for the sheer stubbornness of making it work in the way you’d hoped it would.
But that’s not the only reason you’ll love it. The amount of lights, tinsel and decorations that Clark puts on the house will make your heart sing. Your zodiac sign is ruled by Venus, the planet of possessions, which means you’re kind of extra when it comes to the Christmas decor. You’re a little bougie, Taurus—admit it!
Son of a Nutcracker—Elf is your favorite Christmas movie! In many ways, you’re like Buddy. (Hear me out.) You may be a little unhinged at times, but you’re also incredibly creative and childlike. Just think of Buddy’s over-the-top display at Gimbel’s. If you’re going to do a holiday, you don’t have an “off” switch. Or how about when Buddy tries to express his feelings for Jovie? Even though you talk constantly, when it’s time to get deep, somehow the words get jumbled or you’re 12 again.
On that note, let’s talk about the talking. Ruled by Mercury, the planet of communication, you’ll love all of Buddy’s “elfisms,” like “cotton-headed ninny muggins.” In fact, you’ll probably use that one in casual conversation a few times this season. You’ll also appreciate Buddy’s nonstop talking and mile-a-minute brain. But he’s kind of a cautionary tale: He really can’t stop talking and, as a result, often says the wrong thing, which can happen when you don’t think ahead.
From a purely cinematic perspective, you’ll enjoy the stop-motion animation sequences in the North Pole, a tribute to the classic 1960s specials like Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. You’re not the sentimental type, but you’ll appreciate the details that go into those scenes. Plus, you love a good cartoon!
Home Alone tells a story only a Cancer would truly take to heart: one of family, acceptance and unconditional love. So when Kate, en route to Paris, yells, “Kevin!” after realizing they left their youngest behind, you will feel it in your bones. And shenanigans aside (which we’ll get to in a minute), there’s ultimately nothing more Cancer than the movie’s heartwarming ending, where not one but two characters are reunited with their families: Kevin and also his neighbor, old man Marley. (I’m not crying—you’re crying!)
Your sign is also fiercely protective of your home and the people who are in it. So you’ll be rooting for Kevin as he sets traps to throw off his intruders. A favorite line might be: “This is my home. I have to protect it.” Speaking of those traps—the tar on the steps, the glass ornaments on the floor, the blowtorch—you’ll love that they’re tough but not life-ending. As a Crab, you’re hard on the outside but soft and silly on the inside. So those goofy tactics are just your claws coming out for defense … in painful, yet ultimately harmless, ways.
Leo rules all things magical—children, entertainment and wonder—and this Tim Allen flick is all about rediscovering the joy and magic of Christmas. If there’s one line item in life that you take personal responsibility for, it’s holiday spirit. You’re the one throwing the party, setting up the super-fun kids table, decking the halls, decking yourself and all the rest. Seeing Scott find the holiday spirit once again, not to mention reunite with his son, will tug at your heartstrings.
You’ll also relate to the way Scott acts in the beginning of the movie, since that taps right into Leo’s more negative qualities. Sorry, but it’s true, Leo. He’s self-centered, prideful and lacks accountability. Watching him snap out of that tunnel vision to find himself as THE Santa, you’ll be reminded to get into the Christmas spirit too.
Finally, you love costumes and playing pretend. So seeing a creative version of the North Pole will be right up your alley.
Is seeing truly believing? As a practical earth sign, you may not be all about the miracles, but that’s exactly why this is your movie, Virgo. Ruled by logic-driven Mercury, you just need the facts—and the entire movie is about proving, in a courtroom, that Kris is the real Santa. Something about seeing the judge lean toward belief in the unseen makes you feel like maybe you should too. (Hey, maybe Santa really does exist!)
Since you tend to be more traditional, you’ll also love that this movie is a Yuletide classic, rather than a rambunctious or romantic flick. Being the sensitive and serious sign that you are, you crave meaning and tradition … the way Christmas is supposed to feel. This delivers in spades. And good news: There are two options to choose from. Whether you opt for the classic black-and-white version from the 1940s or the remake from the 1990s, both Miracle on 34th Street movies give you no-fuss, authentic filmmaking that you’re bound to appreciate.
We know you need a little romance with your Christmas, Libra. But in lieu of giving you a generic rom-com, we’re giving you one with serious stakes. Love, Actually covers long-distance relationships, divorce, affairs, grief, loss, unrequited love and risk—and you’ll gobble it all up. It’s the ambiguity and working-it-all-out vibe that resonate with you, because even though you’re a sign that rules love, you don’t always have it figured out. You’ll love watching these couples find their way, perhaps using it as inspiration to work through some of your own relationship problems.
And if you are working through some love issues right now, this movie might just give you the answer you’re looking for. It covers some very specific (and esoteric) holiday-romance questions, such as what to get someone you’ve been married to for decades or whether holidays are the right time to share true feelings. But the question it ultimately aims to answer is one that you’ve been trying to understand your whole life: What is love exactly? We hope this movie helps you find the answer.
Not that you’re a hermit, or living on the top of a mountain over Whoville, but you can definitely relate to the Grinch, Scorpio. With a pessimistic, anti-people attitude, that apt description of his heart (“two sizes too small”) is something you might wonder about yourself during the holidays. And we get it! The best night of the year—Halloween, of course—is over, and you can’t lead with your typical dark vibe and creepy stories while everyone’s talking about “holiday cheer.” But hey, those quirky-looking Whos kind of seem like they stepped out of a Tim Burton movie, so you’ll feel at home here.
Yes, you’re a little macabre for regular Christmas, but that’s because it’s your nature to go deep and want some transformation. This film is perfect for you because it’s about a dying heart that is reborn, offering redemption and the power to start again. Deep down, you know that everyone has a dark and serious side; it’s just that some people (ahem, you) are just more obvious about it. You love the Grinch for owning exactly who he is—no hiding! And ultimately, his transformation and unconditional love are things you want too.
Nothing screams Sagittarius like fleeing your home country after a devastating breakup. Truly, is any holiday movie more relatable? Your sign is ruled by Jupiter, the planet of long-distance travel, new cultures and foreign journeys. So instead of wallowing in emotions (gross), your post-breakup remedy would be to hop on a plane, for sure. In fact, you’re probably one of the only zodiac signs crazy enough to sign up for a house-swapping experiment with a strange woman across the world. It’s a fire-sign thing.
One thing a Sag doesn’t do alone is feelings, so watching with friends is a must. Being a lover of all things funny and awkward, you’ll get a kick out of Jack Black and Kate Winslet’s horrible on-camera chemistry—or fight your friends on it if you’re one of the few believers!
And, of course, who doesn’t watch The Holiday for Jude Law’s character, Graham? Honestly, Graham is kind of perfect for you, given his childlike spirit, giant brain and sexy glasses. Watch at your own risk: You might be booking your next trip to England!
This is a classic story of transformation, humanity and, of course, Christmas spirit. It’s funny, Capricorn— you’re definitely not the Christmas-spirit type. You’re probably too busy at the office to think about decorations. And that’s exactly why watching Ebenezer Scrooge go from a miserly, materialistic grinch to a kind-hearted and giving neighbor will warm your heart … and provide a delicate reminder. After all, you can sometimes lose the plot around what’s important. Honestly, Scrooge is so quintessential Capricorn, you’ll probably start to wonder if this is what you look like to people during the holidays.
Finally, we have to talk about the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Future. Capricorn is ruled by Saturn, the planet of time, aging and consequence. The fact that the ghosts show Scrooge what his life would become if he continues like this reflects Saturn’s lessons about reaping what you sow. Not only will you love the choices he makes from here on in, but you’ll also feel inspired to spread a little more holiday cheer this season.
Every Aquarius (me, included!) loves a good underdog story. That’s why Charlie Brown’s attention to the poor, little reject tree just hits different. Here’s the thing, Aquarius: You tend to feel like an outsider. So when Charlie Brown commits to the tree no one wants, you feel like someone’s choosing you. Charlie Brown himself is a bit of an outsider too, and you’ll love watching how he (and his misfit tree) end up bringing everyone together.
On that note, the very end of the film, when all the kids join hands and sing, is perfectly Aquarius. It’s a representation of what happens when we accept everyone for who they are: authentic harmony. And that’s your speciality!
But perhaps the most quintessential Aquarius trait is to point out flaws in the social system. Yeah, a little intense, but that’s why we need you, Aquarius! You’ll get a kick out of Charlie Brown’s mission to dismantle holiday consumerism. Ultimately, it’s because of everyone’s materialism that he chooses his little tree: to make the point that Christmas is about feelings, not things.
The Polar Express is an ideal choice for Pisces, a sign that wishes they could hop on an imaginary train to an imaginary land pretty much every day. Ruled by Neptune, you live for fantasy and escapism, and your sign also has dominion over dreams. Thanks to this movie’s dreamy animation, it really does feel like a dream you haven’t woken up from yet.
Also, the fact that this little boy is pulled onto the train in the middle of the night gives us the ultimate Piscean question: Is this real or just a dream? You’ll love trying to figure out what to believe and then ultimately trusting the unseen: the magic.
You’ll also really relate with our main character, a lost little soul who feels a bit isolated. (You can see him now, sitting on the train all alone!) Often, you feel this way. Watching him not only reconnect with others on his journey but also find his way back to belief will be a heartwarming way to enjoy Christmas, to say the least.

articles.title: More than 200,000 Carbon Monoxide Detectors Are Being Recalled Due to the Risk of “Serious Injury or Death”—Here’s Which Ones Are a Problem
articles.content:
Some recalls are more serious than others, and this is a serious one. More than 210,000 carbon monoxide and natural gas detectors are being recalled because they can fail to alert consumers to dangerous levels of carbon monoxide, potentially putting people at risk of serious injury or death.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) announced the recall on Wednesday, Nov. 25, involving Steadfast Haven 4-in-1 plug-in CO and natural gas detectors sold by Zenara Commerce LLC.
So, how do you know if you have an affected device? Here’s the scoop.
The recall covers models KH158 and GC03, with approximately 210,410 units affected. The KH158 model is round in shape. It comes in gray or white plastic housing with a black digital display. Meanwhile, the GC03 model is rectangular with a black housing and a black digital display. Consumers can find the model number on the white label on the back of the device, right near the plug.
Consumers purchased the detectors online at Truststeadfast.com between February 2026 and September 2026. They cost around $48 to $70.
The biggest concern is that these devices may not sound an alarm when hazardous levels of carbon monoxide are present. Carbon monoxide is particularly dangerous because it is odorless and colorless, making a functioning detector an important safety device in the home.
According to the CPSC, Zenara has received one report of a detector failing to alarm during a carbon monoxide leak. No injuries have been reported, however.
Consumers should contact Zenara immediately to request a free replacement. The company is asking customers to register at www.truststeadfast.com/pages/recall, mark the recalled detector with the word “RECALLED” and their initials using permanent marker, then upload a photo of the marked product.
Consumers should continue using their recalled detectors until the replacement is installed. Once registration is confirmed, they should dispose of the recalled unit in their household trash.
For additional information, consumers can email recall@truststeadfast.com or visit the company’s recall website. Given the potential consequences, this is one recall homeowners won’t want to overlook.

articles.title: Patrick Stewart Pushed Through Health Struggles to Film Avengers: Doomsday—And It Was “Intensely Emotional”
articles.content: Patrick Stewart gave his final performance everything he had. Nearly a month after the beloved actor’s death at age 86, Avengers: Doomsday directors Joe and Anthony Russo opened up about what it was like working with Stewart as he reprised his iconic role of Professor Charles Xavier one last time. The upcoming Marvel blockbuster, which hits theaters Dec. 18, will mark Stewart’s final onscreen performance. And according to the Russo brothers, the actor’s dedication to his craft was particularly moving given the health challenges he was facing behind the scenes. Speaking with Entertainment Weekly in a piece shared Nov. 24, Anthony recalled how determined Stewart was to give his fellow cast and crew members the best possible experience despite his declining health. “It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence—for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew,” Anthony said. The director explained that Stewart’s commitment went far beyond what was typically expected of an actor arriving on set. “For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.” Stewart’s final day of filming also included a memorable speech to the cast and crew. Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige recalled that the actor seemed aware it might be his last time on a movie set. “He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew,” Feige said. “We didn’t know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was.” Stewart’s family announced his death on Oct. 29, revealing that the actor had died from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. Although Marvel initially offered Stewart roles in both Avengers: Doomsday and its 2027 sequel, Avengers: Secret Wars, he opted to appear only in the former. His final performance will also feature an emotional scene about forgiveness opposite longtime friend and fellow X-Men star Ian McKellen, who returns as Magneto. Feige confirmed that Marvel is currently exploring ways to commemorate Stewart in the upcoming film. “We’re looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend.” Rest in peace, Sir Patrick. articles.title: 12 Common Holiday-Party Disasters—And How to Fix Them ASAP
articles.content:
I entertain a lot around the holidays, and I mean a lot: an annual party with former work colleagues; a Hanukkah dinner (I’m not Jewish, but my crew love latkes); a homemade-pizza night and gingerbread-house-building session with my niece, her BFF and their moms; and, of course, the Feast of the Seven Fishes, the Italian American Christmas Eve tradition.
I’m a planner, and an incredibly organized one, at that. I’ve got spreadsheets with shopping lists, ingredient lists, detailed to-do lists … you get the picture. And yet, no matter how prepared I am, things happen. Like the time I dropped a baking dish of perfectly browned, crispy-edged roasted potatoes on my tile floor, or the time—or, should I say, times?—I ran out of ice. Because here’s the thing: Holiday-party disasters are inevitable. You can plan for every possible scenario, but eventually something will go sideways. And when it does, well, the party must go on.
The trick is knowing how to recover without turning a minor snafu into a major production. As event planner Renee Patrone Rhinehart puts it, “Your guests probably have no idea something went wrong until you start announcing it to everyone.” Her advice? “Just roll with it!”
To find out how to roll with a dozen of the most common holiday-party disasters when you’re hosting, I went to the experts. Iron Chef Alex Guarnaschelli and renowned Southern chef Carla Hall weigh in on turkey troubles and other food emergencies; event planners Rhinehart and Marcy Blum share their secrets for keeping a party on track; etiquette expert Myka Meier offers advice for navigating awkward social situations; and licensed marriage and family therapist Nari Jeter, PhD, weighs in on emotionally charged moments.
So whether your turkey is taking forever to cook, an unexpected guest arrives or your uncle decides today is the perfect time to reignite that family feud, here’s how to save the celebration—and your sanity. Party on!
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, family, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
You’re still getting dressed, the kitchen is a disaster zone, and the appetizers aren’t even out yet. Then the doorbell rings—20 minutes before you expected anyone. Now you need to switch into host mode, and fast.
What to do: Welcome them warmly, offer a drink, and, if you’re comfortable, give them a small task, like putting on the music or lighting candles. “You’re early! Perfect timing. Grab a drink, and help me finish up!” is a perfectly acceptable response, says Rhinehart. My friends know that’s the case at my house: You show up early, and I’m putting you to work.
(For what it’s worth: Meier notes that guests should arrive at the stated time for a seated dinner; for a more casual gathering, arriving 10 to 15 minutes after the start time is generally appropriate.)
Why it works: You don’t need to drop everything to entertain an early arrival. A little hospitality goes a long way, and giving someone a simple job can make them feel included rather than in the way. It can even turn into a bonding moment with your new guest!
You planned dinner for eight, set the table for eight and made just enough food for eight. Then someone shows up with an unexpected plus-one. You could panic about the extra chair and plate, or you could get creative and make it work.
What to do: Take a breath, pull up an extra chair and welcome that person as though you expected them all along. “As a host, your goal is to make everyone feel welcome, even when you’re caught off guard,” says Meier. Simply say, “How lovely to meet you! Come on in.” After all, she adds, “It was not the guest’s fault they were asked to be there, and you don’t want them to feel that when arriving.”
Blum says to have card stock and a pen on hand to make an extra place card, if necessary. Rhinehart recommends stretching the meal with whatever you have—bread, salad or an extra side—and resisting the urge to announce that you weren’t prepared for another person.
Why it works: You’re taking charge, being an excellent hostess and rolling with the surprise. Making a fuss, on the other hand, can turn a small logistical hiccup into an awkward moment. As Rhinehart says, “Nobody needs to know!”
You thought you had everything timed to a T, but the candied yams and green bean casserole are ready, and that dang bird is nowhere close to 165 degrees. Family members are getting hangry, and if you don’t speed this up, you could have a full-fledged holiday meltdown on your hands.
What to do: “This has happened to me, so I know exactly what I’d do!” Hall admits. If dinner is already running late, don’t keep everyone waiting on an intact bird. She recommends breaking it down into pieces and taking the breast off the bone. If there’s room in the oven, cook the white and dark meat in separate pans, since they don’t cook at the same rate. Raise the oven temperature to about 400 degrees Fahrenheit, and use a thermometer to check each piece.
Guarnaschelli has a similar strategy: Take the turkey out of the oven and cut it into pieces, separating the legs and thighs from the breast. Return the breast, still on the bone, to the oven to roast. Place the legs and thighs skin-side-up in a separate pan with a little chicken stock, then let them cook on a separate oven rack. If guests are already waiting, her advice is to put out extra cheese and snacks, smile and keep cooking.
While the turkey finishes, resist the urge to keep all your side dishes in the oven or simmering on the stove. As Guarnaschelli says, “Tin foil is your best friend.” Keep prepared dishes covered with foil on top of the stove to benefit from the oven’s residual heat. “Leaving everything in the oven or simmering on the stove will only overcook and dry everything out.”
Why it works: Breaking down the turkey helps it cook faster, while separating the white and dark meat lets each finish at its own pace. Covering the sides with foil and keeping them near the stove takes advantage of residual heat without overcooking them. Guarnaschelli also points out that items like lasagna, potato gratin and purées in ovenproof dishes “will stay hot longer than you think.”
If you’re worried at all about the bird cooling down while you heat up the side dishes, don’t be. “The turkey doesn’t have to be piping-hot when you carve it,” Hall says. Just make sure the gravy is really hot when you serve it: It will help warm the meat as guests spoon it over their plates.
And don’t throw away the bones. Hall says they can become a beautiful stock for soup or gravy the next day. “But that’s tomorrow’s project,” she adds. “Right now, we’re trying to get dinner on the table!”
You’re halfway through making the mashed potatoes when you realize you’re out of milk. Or butter. Or, heaven forbid, both. Before you abandon the recipe or send someone on an emergency grocery run, take a good look around the kitchen.
What to do: Don’t panic. Instead, figure out whether the missing ingredient is essential to the dish—and if so, how you can potentially substitute another item in its place. Some of the most commonly forgotten staples, Guarnaschelli says, are the simplest: lemons, butter, cream, vinegar and olive oil. If you’re short on butter or milk for mashed potatoes, Hall suggests thinking about what the ingredient contributes—fat, moisture, flavor, structure or texture—and finding a substitute that serves the same purpose. Try sour cream, cream cheese, plain yogurt or grated cheese.
Guarnaschelli agrees that mashed potatoes are particularly forgiving, suggesting cream cheese, sour cream, shredded cheese or buttermilk in place of cream or milk. She also says that if you realize you’re out of nutmeg (say, for butternut squash soup), you can substitute ground cloves. And if you need flavorful stock but don’t have any, water will do in a pinch.
Why it works: A substitute doesn’t need to recreate the original recipe exactly. The key is understanding what the missing ingredient does and finding something that can fill a similar role. As Hall says, “Will they taste exactly like traditional mashed potatoes? No. But different doesn’t mean less delicious.”
Guarnaschelli agrees that there’s almost always a close-enough substitute—and that Thanksgiving guests will have to forgive a little improvisation.
The turkey is carved, the sides are ready to hit the table, and everyone is eager to dig in. Then you taste the gravy and realize it’s saltier than the ocean. Don’t dump it—there’s a way to save it.
What to do: Relax! Your gravy boat won’t sink. Hall recommends making another small batch of gravy without any salt, then combining it with the salty batch to bring the seasoning back into balance. Resist the urge to simply add more stock: It can dilute the flavor and leave you with gravy that’s way too thin.
No more pan drippings? No problem. Hall advises cooking equal parts butter and flour in a separate saucepan to make a roux, then whisking in water or unsalted stock until smooth. “Add this to the salty gravy to increase the volume while keeping it thick and flavorful,” she says.
Why it works: Adding more unsalted gravy reduces the saltiness without sacrificing the rich, savory flavor or consistency you want. And the myth of dropping a raw potato into the pot? Hall says not to bother: It doesn’t selectively absorb salt.
Maybe a joke lands badly, you bring up a sensitive subject or you make an offhand comment that hits a nerve. Suddenly, the conversation goes quiet, and you’re wishing you could push a rewind button on the last 30 seconds. What you say next can make all the difference.
What to do: If you realize you’ve said something hurtful, address it directly. Meier recommends a sincere apology: “I’m so sorry. That came out wrong, and I can see how it could have been hurtful. I sincerely apologize.” Avoid follow-ups like “I’m sorry if you were offended” or “I was only joking!”
Jeter cautions that “the biggest mistake in an emotionally charged situation is to let it escalate.” If you feel embarrassed or defensive, pause before reacting. Take a breath, collect your thoughts and resist the urge to overexplain or justify what you said.
Why it works: A genuine apology acknowledges the impact of your words without making excuses or shifting blame. A brief, sincere response is usually more effective than a lengthy explanation. “During the holidays, emotions can run high, and I don’t think every awkward moment needs to become a big moment,” Meier adds. “A little grace and knowing when to let something go can save an entire evening.”
It happens in a flash: Someone reaches for their glass, knocks it over and sends red wine splashing. Your guest looks mortified, and you’re understandably concerned about the stain. The trick is to handle the mess without making the poor klutz feel even worse.
What to do: “Never make a fuss over a stain while the guests are still there,” says Blum. “It embarrasses them and makes you seem very ungracious.”
Blot the spill immediately with a clean, white towel—don’t rub. Depending on the fabric, cool water may help, but avoid experimenting with random cleaning products, especially on an expensive rug.
Most importantly, reassure the guest. Rhinehart suggests saying, “Don’t worry—everything is fixable!” If they keep apologizing, resist the urge to dwell on the spill. You can even share a story about a time you spilled something at someone else’s home to help them feel less embarrassed.
And if you’re the guest who spilled the wine, apologize, but don’t keep drawing attention to what happened. Rhinehart suggests dropping off upholstery cleaner the next day as a thoughtful gesture. Above all, let the host reassure you and move on. No use crying over spilled, er, wine.
Why it works: Rubbing can push the stain deeper into the fibers. Taking care of the initial spill is important, but spending the rest of the party on your hands and knees cleaning it only makes the incident feel bigger than it is. As Rhinehart says, “It’s a party. Things spill. That’s life!”
You just wanted to host a nice holiday dinner, but somehow Uncle Steve and your cousin are rehashing a family feud that’s older than some of the guests around the table. Voices are getting louder, everyone else is getting uncomfortable, and the turkey is no longer the main event. Time for you to step in.
What to do: If you’re the host, step in without taking sides. Jeter suggests acknowledging the disagreement and redirecting the conversation: “I can tell this is important to both of you, but it’s not going to be solved here. Let’s set it aside for now and enjoy our time together.” If the argument continues to escalate, be firmer (while still keeping your cool): “Things are getting heated. You’re going to have to discuss this somewhere else after dinner.”
If you’re personally being pulled into the disagreement, Jeter recommends pausing rather than reacting defensively. Take a breath, count to 10 or step away for a moment. You can also establish a boundary by saying, “I don’t feel comfortable talking about that right now.”
Why it works: You can set the tone for your gathering without becoming the referee. Jeter advises resisting the urge to get defensive, overexplain or counterattack. “When someone has invited us to a fight, we’re not obligated to show up,” she says. You don’t need to convince someone to agree with you or resolve a long-standing family disagreement over dinner. Sometimes the best response is simply to change the subject and enjoy the rest of the evening.
It’s been a long day, the house is loud, and there’s a lot more excitement than usual. Then a child starts crying, running around or refusing to cooperate, and tension builds. Whether it’s your kid or someone else’s, you’ll want to address the behavior without adding to the chaos.
What to do: Holiday gatherings can be particularly overstimulating for children, Jeter notes, especially when familiar routines, sleep schedules and surroundings are disrupted. New sights, sounds, smells and people can all contribute to a child’s distress.
If it’s your child who’s having a hard time, step away from the party and tend to them. Don’t be afraid to ask someone to take over hosting duties for a few minutes.
If someone else’s child is acting out, Jeter recommends setting a simple household boundary. For example: “We don’t take those drinks in the living room, but you’re welcome to sit at the table and drink it.” If the behavior continues or poses a safety concern, speak privately with the parent and be specific about what’s happening. You might say, “Jack is running around the hot stove, and I’m worried he’ll get hurt. Could you help me keep the kids out of the kitchen?”
Why it works: Kids can struggle to manage all the excitement and stimulation of a holiday gathering. Stepping away from the action can give them a chance to reset. Jeter emphasizes that parents shouldn’t feel obligated to prioritize hosting over caring for their child. When another child is involved, focus on the specific behavior rather than criticizing the child or parent, so you can address the problem without creating additional tension.
The meal was great (if you do say so yourself) and the plates have been cleared, but suddenly everyone seems to have run out of things to say. Maybe the conversation has stalled or everyone has retreated into smaller groups. You don’t need to break out the icebreaker cards, but a little nudge can get things moving again.
What to do: You don’t need to announce the lull or make a big production of getting everyone talking again. Rhinehart recommends keeping a few easy conversation starters in your back pocket and introducing them naturally. For example, you might say, “I was wondering, what vacations do you all have coming up? I love to hear other people’s plans to spark my own ideas!” Or try asking everyone to share the highlight of their year or whether they’ve seen any good movies lately. These questions work just as well when guests are mingling before or after dinner as they do when everyone is seated.
You can also change the setting if the energy needs a boost: Move everyone into the living room for dessert or another cocktail, or put on a fun playlist. If you have an outgoing friend at the table, enlist their help. And when introducing guests to one another, look for people who have something in common.
Why it works: A lull doesn’t mean the party is failing. Sometimes people just need an easy opening or a little help finding common ground. The key is to keep things casual and avoid making guests feel as though they’re being put on the spot.
Remember, not everyone wants to participate in a game or answer a question right then and there. “Nobody wants to feel like they’re at a corporate team-building retreat when they came over for dinner!” Rhinehart cautions. Keep things light, follow your guests’ lead and don’t force it.
One guest has had a little too much to drink, and it’s starting to show. They’re getting loud, picking fights or making other guests uncomfortable. You don’t want to embarrass anyone or derail the evening, but you also can’t let one person’s behavior ruin the party.
What to do: Approach the guest privately and with care, not criticism. Jeter suggests saying, “Hey, I’m concerned about you. You didn’t seem like yourself in there. I want to make sure you’re OK.”
If they’re intoxicated, don’t expect a productive conversation. Offer water, a quiet place to sit and help arranging a safe ride home. If necessary, set a clear boundary: “I care about you, but it’s not a good idea for you to stay. How can you safely get home?”
Why it works: The goal is to address the behavior without humiliating anyone. Jeter recommends approaching the situation with compassion, but that doesn’t mean you have to tolerate disruptive or unsafe behavior. “We all hope family gatherings will go well, but we can also be mentally and emotionally prepared to manage our feelings and set boundaries if things don’t go well,” she adds.
And remember, you don’t need everyone to agree with your decision for it to be valid. If a guest makes others uncomfortable or creates a safety issue, it’s OK to ask them to leave.
A guest shows up to your holiday party with a beautifully wrapped present, and you weren’t expecting gifts—let alone prepared to give one in return. Now you’re scrambling to figure out how to respond without making things awkward or turning their thoughtful gesture into an uncomfortable moment.
What to do: Resist the urge to announce, “Oh, no! I didn’t get you anything!” Instead, Meier suggests saying, “This is so incredibly thoughtful of you! What a lovely surprise. Thank you for thinking of me!” You don’t need to promise a gift in return. A handwritten thank-you note afterward is a lovely gesture.
Why it works: Calling attention to the imbalance can make the giver feel awkward about a gesture that was meant to be kind. Accept the gift graciously, and let the moment be about their thoughtfulness—not what you did or didn’t buy.
Having a successful holiday party isn’t about executing every detail perfectly. It’s about making people feel comfortable, included and happy to be there. As Hall reminds us: “Your guests aren’t coming to judge your cooking. They’re coming to spend time with you!”
Blum recommends staying flexible and remembering that you don’t have to be a superhero host. She also has one very practical tip for avoiding a common party hiccup: “Buy extra, and then buy another bag!” (Yes, she’s talking about ice.)
And Guarnaschelli offers perhaps the best advice of all: “I find honesty and laughing at yourself is the best thing you can do in a situation like this.” After all, she points out, everyone who’s hosted a holiday dinner has experienced pitfalls and made mistakes. Sometimes, those mishaps even add laughter and levity to the evening.
So make the backup plan, ask for help when you need it and don’t spend the entire party hiding in the kitchen. And if, like me, you send the roasted potatoes crashing to the floor, take a breath and remember that a little accident isn’t the end of the party. Pour yourself a drink, sit down with your guests and enjoy the gathering you’ve worked so hard to bring together. After all, the best memories rarely come from the things that went perfectly.

Some of the most commonly forgotten staples, Guarnaschelli says, are the simplest: lemons, butter, cream, vinegar and olive oil. If you’re short on butter or milk for mashed potatoes, Hall suggests thinking about what the ingredient contributes—fat, moisture, flavor, structure or texture—and finding a substitute that serves the same purpose. Try sour cream, cream cheese, plain yogurt or grated cheese.

Guarnaschelli agrees that mashed potatoes are particularly forgiving, suggesting cream cheese, sour cream, shredded cheese or buttermilk in place of cream or milk. She also says that if you realize you’re out of nutmeg (say, for butternut squash soup), you can substitute ground cloves. And if you need flavorful stock but don’t have any, water will do in a pinch.

Why it works: A substitute doesn’t need to recreate the original recipe exactly. The key is understanding what the missing ingredient does and finding something that can fill a similar role. As Hall says, “Will they taste exactly like traditional mashed potatoes? No. But different doesn’t mean less delicious.”

Guarnaschelli agrees that there’s almost always a close-enough substitute—and that Thanksgiving guests will have to forgive a little improvisation.

The gravy is too salty

The turkey is carved, the sides are ready to hit the table, and everyone is eager to dig in. Then you taste the gravy and realize it’s saltier than the ocean. Don’t dump it—there’s a way to save it.

What to do: Relax! Your gravy boat won’t sink. Hall recommends making another small batch of gravy without any salt, then combining it with the salty batch to bring the seasoning back into balance. Resist the urge to simply add more stock: It can dilute the flavor and leave you with gravy that’s way too thin.

No more pan drippings? No problem. Hall advises cooking equal parts butter and flour in a separate saucepan to make a roux, then whisking in water or unsalted stock until smooth. “Add this to the salty gravy to increase the volume while keeping it thick and flavorful,” she says.

Why it works: Adding more unsalted gravy reduces the saltiness without sacrificing the rich, savory flavor or consistency you want. And the myth of dropping a raw potato into the pot? Hall says not to bother: It doesn’t selectively absorb salt.

You say the wrong thing

Maybe a joke lands badly, you bring up a sensitive subject or you make an offhand comment that hits a nerve. Suddenly, the conversation goes quiet, and you’re wishing you could push a rewind button on the last 30 seconds. What you say next can make all the difference.

What to do: If you realize you’ve said something hurtful, address it directly. Meier recommends a sincere apology: “I’m so sorry. That came out wrong, and I can see how it could have been hurtful. I sincerely apologize.” Avoid follow-ups like “I’m sorry if you were offended” or “I was only joking!”

Jeter cautions that “the biggest mistake in an emotionally charged situation is to let it escalate.” If you feel embarrassed or defensive, pause before reacting. Take a breath, collect your thoughts and resist the urge to overexplain or justify what you said.

Why it works: A genuine apology acknowledges the impact of your words without making excuses or shifting blame. A brief, sincere response is usually more effective than a lengthy explanation. “During the holidays, emotions can run high, and I don’t think every awkward moment needs to become a big moment,” Meier adds. “A little grace and knowing when to let something go can save an entire evening.”

Someone spills red wine on your couch or rug

It happens in a flash: Someone reaches for their glass, knocks it over and sends red wine splashing. Your guest looks mortified, and you’re understandably concerned about the stain. The trick is to handle the mess without making the poor klutz feel even worse.

What to do: “Never make a fuss over a stain while the guests are still there,” says Blum. “It embarrasses them and makes you seem very ungracious.”

Blot the spill immediately with a clean, white towel—don’t rub. Depending on the fabric, cool water may help, but avoid experimenting with random cleaning products, especially on an expensive rug.

Most importantly, reassure the guest. Rhinehart suggests saying, “Don’t worry—everything is fixable!” If they keep apologizing, resist the urge to dwell on the spill. You can even share a story about a time you spilled something at someone else’s home to help them feel less embarrassed.

And if you’re the guest who spilled the wine, apologize, but don’t keep drawing attention to what happened. Rhinehart suggests dropping off upholstery cleaner the next day as a thoughtful gesture. Above all, let the host reassure you and move on. No use crying over spilled, er, wine.

Why it works: Rubbing can push the stain deeper into the fibers. Taking care of the initial spill is important, but spending the rest of the party on your hands and knees cleaning it only makes the incident feel bigger than it is. As Rhinehart says, “It’s a party. Things spill. That’s life!”

A family argument breaks out at the table

You just wanted to host a nice holiday dinner, but somehow Uncle Steve and your cousin are rehashing a family feud that’s older than some of the guests around the table. Voices are getting louder, everyone else is getting uncomfortable, and the turkey is no longer the main event. Time for you to step in.

What to do: If you’re the host, step in without taking sides. Jeter suggests acknowledging the disagreement and redirecting the conversation: “I can tell this is important to both of you, but it’s not going to be solved here. Let’s set it aside for now and enjoy our time together.” If the argument continues to escalate, be firmer (while still keeping your cool): “Things are getting heated. You’re going to have to discuss this somewhere else after dinner.”

If you’re personally being pulled into the disagreement, Jeter recommends pausing rather than reacting defensively. Take a breath, count to 10 or step away for a moment. You can also establish a boundary by saying, “I don’t feel comfortable talking about that right now.”

Why it works: You can set the tone for your gathering without becoming the referee. Jeter advises resisting the urge to get defensive, overexplain or counterattack. “When someone has invited us to a fight, we’re not obligated to show up,” she says. You don’t need to convince someone to agree with you or resolve a long-standing family disagreement over dinner. Sometimes the best response is simply to change the subject and enjoy the rest of the evening.

A child is having a meltdown

It’s been a long day, the house is loud, and there’s a lot more excitement than usual. Then a child starts crying, running around or refusing to cooperate, and tension builds. Whether it’s your kid or someone else’s, you’ll want to address the behavior without adding to the chaos.

What to do: Holiday gatherings can be particularly overstimulating for children, Jeter notes, especially when familiar routines, sleep schedules and surroundings are disrupted. New sights, sounds, smells and people can all contribute to a child’s distress.

If it’s your child who’s having a hard time, step away from the party and tend to them. Don’t be afraid to ask someone to take over hosting duties for a few minutes.

If someone else’s child is acting out, Jeter recommends setting a simple household boundary. For example: “We don’t take those drinks in the living room, but you’re welcome to sit at the table and drink it.” If the behavior continues or poses a safety concern, speak privately with the parent and be specific about what’s happening. You might say, “Jack is running around the hot stove, and I’m worried he’ll get hurt. Could you help me keep the kids out of the kitchen?”

Why it works: Kids can struggle to manage all the excitement and stimulation of a holiday gathering. Stepping away from the action can give them a chance to reset. Jeter emphasizes that parents shouldn’t feel obligated to prioritize hosting over caring for their child. When another child is involved, focus on the specific behavior rather than criticizing the child or parent, so you can address the problem without creating additional tension.

The conversation runs dry

The meal was great (if you do say so yourself) and the plates have been cleared, but suddenly everyone seems to have run out of things to say. Maybe the conversation has stalled or everyone has retreated into smaller groups. You don’t need to break out the icebreaker cards, but a little nudge can get things moving again.

What to do: You don’t need to announce the lull or make a big production of getting everyone talking again. Rhinehart recommends keeping a few easy conversation starters in your back pocket and introducing them naturally. For example, you might say, “I was wondering, what vacations do you all have coming up? I love to hear other people’s plans to spark my own ideas!” Or try asking everyone to share the highlight of their year or whether they’ve seen any good movies lately. These questions work just as well when guests are mingling before or after dinner as they do when everyone is seated.

You can also change the setting if the energy needs a boost: Move everyone into the living room for dessert or another cocktail, or put on a fun playlist. If you have an outgoing friend at the table, enlist their help. And when introducing guests to one another, look for people who have something in common.

Why it works: A lull doesn’t mean the party is failing. Sometimes people just need an easy opening or a little help finding common ground. The key is to keep things casual and avoid making guests feel as though they’re being put on the spot.

Remember, not everyone wants to participate in a game or answer a question right then and there. “Nobody wants to feel like they’re at a corporate team-building retreat when they came over for dinner!” Rhinehart cautions. Keep things light, follow your guests’ lead and don’t force it. 

An adult guest gets drunk or disruptive

One guest has had a little too much to drink, and it’s starting to show. They’re getting loud, picking fights or making other guests uncomfortable. You don’t want to embarrass anyone or derail the evening, but you also can’t let one person’s behavior ruin the party.

What to do: Approach the guest privately and with care, not criticism. Jeter suggests saying, “Hey, I’m concerned about you. You didn’t seem like yourself in there. I want to make sure you’re OK.”

If they’re intoxicated, don’t expect a productive conversation. Offer water, a quiet place to sit and help arranging a safe ride home. If necessary, set a clear boundary: “I care about you, but it’s not a good idea for you to stay. How can you safely get home?”

Why it works: The goal is to address the behavior without humiliating anyone. Jeter recommends approaching the situation with compassion, but that doesn’t mean you have to tolerate disruptive or unsafe behavior. “We all hope family gatherings will go well, but we can also be mentally and emotionally prepared to manage our feelings and set boundaries if things don’t go well,” she adds.

And remember, you don’t need everyone to agree with your decision for it to be valid. If a guest makes others uncomfortable or creates a safety issue, it’s OK to ask them to leave. 

Someone gives you a gift—and you didn’t get them one

A guest shows up to your holiday party with a beautifully wrapped present, and you weren’t expecting gifts—let alone prepared to give one in return. Now you’re scrambling to figure out how to respond without making things awkward or turning their thoughtful gesture into an uncomfortable moment.

What to do: Resist the urge to announce, “Oh, no! I didn’t get you anything!” Instead, Meier suggests saying, “This is so incredibly thoughtful of you! What a lovely surprise. Thank you for thinking of me!” You don’t need to promise a gift in return. A handwritten thank-you note afterward is a lovely gesture.

Why it works: Calling attention to the imbalance can make the giver feel awkward about a gesture that was meant to be kind. Accept the gift graciously, and let the moment be about their thoughtfulness—not what you did or didn’t buy.

The bottom line

Having a successful holiday party isn’t about executing every detail perfectly. It’s about making people feel comfortable, included and happy to be there. As Hall reminds us: “Your guests aren’t coming to judge your cooking. They’re coming to spend time with you!”

Blum recommends staying flexible and remembering that you don’t have to be a superhero host. She also has one very practical tip for avoiding a common party hiccup: “Buy extra, and then buy another bag!” (Yes, she’s talking about ice.)

And Guarnaschelli offers perhaps the best advice of all: “I find honesty and laughing at yourself is the best thing you can do in a situation like this.” After all, she points out, everyone who’s hosted a holiday dinner has experienced pitfalls and made mistakes. Sometimes, those mishaps even add laughter and levity to the evening.

So make the backup plan, ask for help when you need it and don’t spend the entire party hiding in the kitchen. And if, like me, you send the roasted potatoes crashing to the floor, take a breath and remember that a little accident isn’t the end of the party. Pour yourself a drink, sit down with your guests and enjoy the gathering you’ve worked so hard to bring together. After all, the best memories rarely come from the things that went perfectly.

articles.title: More Than a Dozen Injectable Meds Are Being Recalled Due to a “Life-Threatening” Health Risk—Here’s the Full List
articles.content:
A nationwide recall is affecting more than a dozen types of injectable medications after concerns came up about whether the products are sterile. It covers 261 lots of compounded medications, and while no contamination has been found, the worry is a serious one. An injectable drug that isn’t sterile can cause serious infections.
Greenwich Rx, a 503A compounding pharmacy based in Tomball, Texas, announced the voluntary recall on Friday, Nov. 20. The affected medications were sold under the Greenwich Rx name, while some were compounded for another pharmacy, Clove Rx. The recall follows an FDA inspection and the company’s own evaluation of its products.
The affected products were dispensed nationwide between Aug. 10 and Sept. 21, 2026. Here’s the list of the 13 types of injectable medications included in the recall:
Some combination products also contain peptides such as BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu and KPV.
“Use of a drug product intended to be sterile, that is not sterile, could result in serious infections, which may be life threatening,” the official risk statement in the FDA recall notice states.
The good news is that Greenwich Rx says it hasn’t received reports of related adverse events. But as with many recalls, the action is being carried out as a precaution.
Consumers can find the full list of affected products, including strengths, lot numbers and beyond-use dates, on the Greenwich Rx recall notice. Remember to check the information against the label on your medication rather than assuming a product is safe based on its name alone.
Anyone with an affected product should stop using it immediately and discard it, as with many recalls. Greenwich Rx is contacting customers by mail, but people who received medications through Clove Rx should check the recall list even if they haven’t received a notice.
Consumers with questions can direct them to Sedgwick at 888-243-5547 or GreenwichRx6588@sedgwick.com, Monday through Friday, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET.
Anyone who experiences a health problem that may be related to one of these medications should contact their healthcare provider. People can also report adverse reactions to the FDA through its MedWatch program.
